# Draft:Cornelius Crane Pacific Expedition

The Cornelius Crane Pacific Expedition was privately sponsored by Cornelius Vanderbilt Crane, and the Field Museum of Natural History institutionally sponsored the expedition. Beginning November of 1928, the expedition, led by Cornelius Crane in the Illyria yacht, covered over 30,000 miles along the South Pacific, coasts along Asia, North Pacific, and west coasts of Canada. The expedition was funded primarily with the intent of making an accurate record of specimens and obtaining particular specimens such as sea serpents, cassowaries, cormorants, as well as an array of different reptiles and amphibians. When their expedition ended in late September of 1929, they brought back with them over 16,000 specimens.
Funding
Cornelius Vanderbilt Crane (1905 - 1962) was a benefactor of the Field Museum of Natural History and known philanthropist with an interest in exploring the world. The expedition was initially planned to be a trip for pleasure, but Cornelius Crane offered to fund it for the Field Museum. With his money, he funded his most well known traveling expedition, the Cornelius Crane Pacific Expedition. The expedition was also credited as being institutionally sponsored by the Field Museum.
Crew
With Cornelius Crane as the leader of this expedition, the appointed Head of Scientific Staff was Karl P. Schmidt and the Captain/Navigator was Seldon B. Boutilier — holding 30 years of experience at sea. Through the addition of Walter A. Weber, appointed to be illustrator as well as one of the collectors in the crew, Crane hoped to achieve his goal of an accurate record of specimens through having an illustrator on board. Joining the crew as well was William L. Moss, who served as a physician. He was a bacteriologist and immunologist who wanted to study tropical diseases and blood types while on the expedition.  Sidney N. Shurcliff was a friend of Cornelius Crane and photographed and filmed much of the expedition. He was credited as being one of the first photographers to successfully film underwater coral, which he did during the expedition at some reefs at the Tropics of Capricorn.
Expedition journey
Illyria construction and departure
The yacht was built with the expedition in mind. Cornelius Crane Sr. gifted it's construction to his son. The yacht was built to accommodate the space required for the scientific expedition. On September 14th, 1928, the Illyria was brought from Italy to New York. The yacht set sail the next month, after stocking the yacht with the necessary supplies, on November 16th.
Route
Throughout the route, the Illyria experienced trouble with radio messages.

Illyria return
After 11 months, the Illyria arrived at Boston on October 16th, 1929. It was a total of 32,000 nautical miles.
Notable collections
The specimens collected during this expedition was then given to the Field Museum of Natural History upon their return. On the expedition there was a total of 881 mammals, 1,200 birds, 12,000 fishes, 1,075 insects, 500 crustaceans, 300 mollusks, 100 worms, 50 echinoderms, and 2,008 reptiles and amphibians collected.
Birds
At the time of the expedition the cassowary was still a fairly new "discovery" for the Field Museum of Natural History. More information and research was desired to be collected on cassowaries. The Crane Pacific Expedition collected some specimen of cassowaries. Those on board the Illyria talked about consuming the cassowary meat during the expedition.
Fish
There was one new family, seven new genera, one new subgenus, and 51 new species collected.
Mammals
Frank C. Wonder, collector and taxidermist on the expedition, collected all four of the only specimens recorded of the Darwin's Galápagos mouse on the Galapagos Islands from the 12-16th of January 1929.
Reptiles and amphibians
The New Guinea Crocodile (Crocodylus novaeguineae) was announced to be a new species discovered by the Field Museum of Natural History.Schmidt,  Karl Patterson. Notes on New Guinean Crocodiles. 1932, .
